_meta.about: Modern verdicts on Culpeper's herbs. Looked up by herb id; never generated by a model at runtime.
_meta.status: DRAFT written from general knowledge, not yet checked line by line against primary sources. Review before publishing.

tags.Folklore: No good evidence it works as claimed.
tags.Plausible: Some real pharmacology or clinical evidence supports a version of the claim.
tags.Harmful: Can cause real injury. May also have some use.

_meta.toxicity: low | moderate | high: how much harm the plant itself can do if swallowed or misused, independent of the tag.

fox-glove.summary: Contains cardiac glycosides, the source of the heart drug digoxin. Real medicine, but in the raw plant the gap between a treatment and a fatal poisoning is perilously thin.
fox-glove.caution: Every part is poisonous, including leaves that are easily mistaken for comfrey.

hemlock.summary: Contains coniine, which paralyses the muscles used for breathing. It is the classical poison of ancient Greek executions, traditionally linked to Socrates.
hemlock.caution: No safe way to use it at home. Often confused with wild carrot, parsley and wild fennel.

henbane.summary: Rich in tropane alkaloids (hyoscyamine, scopolamine) that cause delirium, hallucinations and dangerous heart effects. Folklore ties it to witches' 'flying ointments'. Purified scopolamine is still used for motion sickness.
henbane.caution: Poisoning causes confusion and agitation that can last for days.

black-hellebore.summary: Ancient healers used hellebore as a purge and a cure for madness. It contains cardiac glycosides and irritant saponins, and swallowing it risks vomiting, slowed heartbeat and serious heart rhythm problems.
black-hellebore.caution: A garden plant that is toxic if eaten, including by pets.

nightshade.summary: A relative of belladonna, not the same plant. Unripe berries and leaves contain toxic glycoalkaloids that cause stomach upset and drowsiness, and children are most at risk. Culpeper's cooling poultices have no modern support.
nightshade.caution: Do not confuse it with deadly nightshade (belladonna), which is far more dangerous.

amara-dulcis.summary: Culpeper recommended it to 'remove witchcraft'. No evidence for that. The red berries contain solanine-type toxins that can cause vomiting, drowsiness and, in children, more serious poisoning.
amara-dulcis.caution: The berries look tempting to children. Keep away from them.

lily-of-the-valley.summary: Contains cardiac glycosides similar to foxglove's. Eating the leaves, flowers or berries can disturb the heartbeat dangerously, and even the water from a vase of the flowers is considered hazardous.
lily-of-the-valley.caution: Looks gentle, poisons seriously. Often confused with wild garlic leaves.

english-tobacco.summary: Culpeper prescribed it for many ailments. It contains nicotine, which is addictive and toxic, and smoking tobacco is the leading preventable cause of death worldwide. No modern medicine uses the raw leaf.
english-tobacco.caution: Nicotine can be absorbed through skin and by swallowing leaf material.

pennyroyal.summary: Its oil contains pulegone, which can cause severe liver and kidney damage. Culpeper writes of it bringing on women's courses; that old use as an abortifacient has led to documented deaths.
pennyroyal.caution: Never use pennyroyal oil internally. Avoid the herb altogether in pregnancy.

savine.summary: A toxic juniper whose oil irritates the gut and kidneys. It was a notorious old abortifacient and has caused fatal poisonings.
savine.caution: Not the same as common juniper berries.

poppy.modern_name: Opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) and corn poppy
poppy.summary: Culpeper's praise of poppy for sleep and pain has real pharmacology behind it: the opium poppy is the source of morphine and codeine. But raw preparations vary wildly in strength, and overdose stops breathing. The red corn poppy is much milder.
poppy.caution: Homemade poppy preparations have killed people, especially children.

cuckow-point.summary: The fresh plant contains needle-like calcium oxalate crystals that burn the mouth and throat. Culpeper's remedies using it have no modern support. The red berries attract children.
cuckow-point.caution: Swallowing causes painful swelling of the mouth and throat.

wormwood.summary: A genuine bitter that stimulates digestion, which fits Culpeper's use of it for the stomach. The 'worms' claim is not well supported for this species (the antimalarial artemisinin comes from a relative). It contains thujone, the compound in absinthe, which is neurotoxic in quantity.
wormwood.caution: Avoid in pregnancy and with a history of seizures.

garden-rue.summary: Once carried as protection against plague and witchcraft. Its sap makes skin hypersensitive to sunlight and can cause blisters and burns, and eating it can harm the liver and kidneys.
garden-rue.caution: Handle with gloves, and avoid in pregnancy.

garden-tansy.summary: Rich in thujone, which is toxic to the nervous system and liver. Once used for worms and to affect pregnancy, tansy is now considered unsafe to swallow, and the oil has caused poisonings.

darnel.summary: A grass whose seeds are often infected with a fungus that produces toxic compounds. Bread contaminated with it caused dizziness, trembling and vomiting, which is why the species name means 'drunken'.
darnel.caution: Its toxicity depends on fungal infection, so safety cannot be judged by looking at it.

comfrey.summary: Creams made from it have some trial support for bruises and sprains, which matches its old name 'knitbone'. Taken internally it contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can damage the liver, and oral products are restricted in several countries.
comfrey.caution: Do not swallow it. Do not put it on broken skin for long periods.

coltsfoot.summary: The soothing mucilage in the leaves fits its old use for coughs (Tussilago means 'cough dispeller'). But some plants contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids that are toxic to the liver, which is why it is no longer recommended for regular internal use.
coltsfoot.caution: Not advised for regular use, in pregnancy, or with liver disease.

elder-tree.summary: Cooked elderberry extracts have some evidence for shortening cold and flu symptoms. The raw berries, leaves, bark and stems contain compounds that release cyanide and cause nausea and vomiting.
elder-tree.caution: Cook the berries. Never eat raw elderberries or use the leaves or bark.

dwarf-elder.summary: A smaller, more toxic relative of the elder. The berries act as a purge and an emetic, and it is not used in modern medicine.
dwarf-elder.caution: Not interchangeable with the common elder.

misselto.summary: Culpeper, like earlier herbalists, used it for the falling sickness (epilepsy). There is no good evidence it helps. The berries and leaves contain toxic proteins, and eating them can cause stomach and heart problems.
misselto.caution: The sticky white berries are poisonous. Keep them away from children and pets.

st-john-s-wort.summary: Trials support it for mild to moderate depression, so Culpeper's use for a troubled mind is not baseless. Its real danger is interactions: it weakens many medicines, including contraceptives, blood thinners and antidepressants. It also increases sun sensitivity.
st-john-s-wort.caution: Talk to a pharmacist before combining it with any prescription medicine.

garden-valerian.summary: Widely used for sleep. Trial evidence is mixed but suggests a modest effect for some people. The smell of the root is famously unpleasant, and cats are fond of it.
garden-valerian.caution: Can cause drowsiness. Avoid combining with alcohol or sedatives.

camomile.summary: Mildly calming, and a gentle digestive comfort. There is some trial evidence for anxiety and for soothing the stomach. It is among the safer herbs on this list.
camomile.caution: Can trigger allergy in people sensitive to ragweed and the daisy family.

balm.summary: Small trials suggest it can ease mild anxiety and promote calm, which fits Culpeper's claim that it makes the heart merry. The evidence is limited but encouraging.
balm.caution: May cause drowsiness. Check with a doctor if you have a thyroid condition.

feverfew.summary: Studied for preventing migraines, with mixed results but some positive trials. It works better as a preventive than as a fever remedy, despite the name.
feverfew.caution: Avoid in pregnancy. Chewing the leaves can cause mouth sores.

garlick.summary: Garlic has real antimicrobial activity in the lab and may modestly lower blood pressure. It cannot cure disease or ward off plague, whatever the folklore says.
garlick.caution: In large amounts it can thin the blood. Tell your surgeon about heavy use.

nettles.summary: Nutritious when cooked, which removes the sting. Leaf extracts have been studied for hay fever and joint pain, and the root for prostate symptoms, with modest results.
nettles.caution: Use gloves. Nettle can interact with blood pressure and blood-thinning medicines.

dandelion.summary: A mild diuretic and a bitter that may aid digestion, with limited human evidence. It is safe as a food for most people.
dandelion.caution: Can cause allergy in people sensitive to the daisy family.

rosemary.summary: Long called the herb of remembrance. A few small studies hint that its aroma may affect alertness and recall, but the evidence is weak. It is a lovely, safe kitchen herb either way.
rosemary.caution: Large medicinal amounts are not advised in pregnancy.

marigolds.summary: Calendula creams have small trial support for skin irritation and wound healing. It is not the Mexican cempasuchil (Tagetes), though both are called marigold.
marigolds.caution: Can trigger allergy in people sensitive to the daisy family.

yarrow.summary: Called a wound herb since antiquity, and the leaves do contain astringent compounds. Clinical evidence for stopping bleeding is lacking, so do not rely on it for a real wound.
yarrow.caution: Can trigger allergy in people sensitive to the daisy family. Avoid in pregnancy.

hops.summary: Mildly sedating, and often paired with valerian in sleep products. Evidence is modest, and it fits Culpeper's use for quieting the body.
hops.caution: Can add to drowsiness. Avoid with depression unless a doctor agrees.

mint.summary: Peppermint oil in enteric-coated capsules has good trial evidence for irritable bowel symptoms. Mint tea is a safe, soothing comfort for upset stomachs.
mint.caution: Can worsen acid reflux. Do not apply mint oil to the face of babies.

sage.summary: Small trials suggest benefits for sore throats and mild memory effects, which fits its old reputation as a herb of wisdom. Common sage contains some thujone, so avoid very large amounts.
sage.caution: Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy and with epilepsy.

willow-tree.summary: Willow bark contains salicin, the natural ancestor of aspirin, so its use for pain and fever is real. Extracts show modest pain relief for back pain and arthritis.
willow-tree.caution: Behaves like aspirin. Avoid in children and with aspirin allergy or blood thinners.

mugwort.summary: A herb of dreams and protection in European folklore. Good evidence for its medicinal claims is lacking. It is related to wormwood and contains thujone.
mugwort.caution: Not safe in pregnancy. Can trigger allergy in people sensitive to the daisy family.

eyebright.summary: Named for its supposed benefit to sight, but there is little good evidence it helps eye conditions.
eyebright.caution: Do not put homemade herbal drops or washes in your eyes. Contaminated preparations can cause infection.

thyme.summary: Contains thymol, a real antiseptic used in mouthwashes, and thyme preparations have been studied for coughs. A fine kitchen herb with a respectable medicinal side.
thyme.caution: Concentrated thyme oil can burn skin and must be diluted.

lavender.summary: Lavender aroma and a standardised oral preparation have both been studied for anxiety, with encouraging if limited results.
lavender.caution: Lavender oil is for diluted skin use or aroma, not for swallowing.

wood-betony.summary: Once prized as a cure-all, so much so that the Romans said 'sell your coat and buy betony'. Modern evidence for its claimed effects is thin.
wood-betony.caution: Little is known about its safety in medicinal amounts.

hawthorn.summary: Hawthorn extracts have been studied as an add-on treatment for mild heart failure, which fits its old reputation as a heart herb. It is not a substitute for medical care.
hawthorn.caution: Can interact with heart and blood pressure medicines. Do not self-treat heart problems.

celandine.summary: Its orange sap is a folk wart treatment, and there is some lab evidence of activity. Swallowed products have been linked to liver injury, and the sap can irritate skin.
celandine.caution: Do not take it internally. Avoid contact with eyes.

dog-mercury.summary: Contains compounds that irritate the gut and are toxic to people and livestock. Culpeper himself doubted it, and it has no place in modern medicine.
dog-mercury.caution: Do not eat it. It is sometimes mistaken for edible greens.

french-and-dog-mercury.modern_name: French mercury (Mercurialis annua) and dog's mercury
french-and-dog-mercury.summary: Both plants contain compounds that irritate the gut and can poison people and animals. Culpeper recommended them as purges and for other ills, but neither has modern use.

briony.summary: Culpeper says it purges 'with great violence', and he is right. The root and red berries contain cucurbitacins that cause severe vomiting, diarrhoea and in some cases serious poisoning.
briony.caution: Poisoning has occurred in children who ate the berries.
